newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Forecasting NZ interest and exchange rates.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Forecasting NZ interest and exchange rates.

text.p: By Anthony Byett, Economist at ASB Bank Ltd.
WELLINGTON, Nov 20 - Picking exchange rates and interest rates has always been interesting and is certainly not an art or science (whichever it is) for the complacent.
John Kenneth Galbraith once put forecasters into two classes: those who don't know...and those who don't know they don't know.

This seems particularly pertinent at the moment when one thinks of the widespread discussion and concern about New Zealand inflationary and political risks over the last few months when, at the end of the day, the major driving force in
the New Zealand financial markets came to be the swell of offshore investment.
Plot NZ interest rates alongside those of other high yielding currencies and the trend is quite clear.
It seems Japanese investors' appetite for risk increased significantly in recent months, not the least because of their persistently low domestic interest rates.

This is yet another example of unforseen "shocks" providing the ultimate influence to changes in exchange rates and interest rates. Put another way, current interest rates and exchange rates already have current information priced into rates.
The trick -- and hence the confusion whether an art or a science -- is for forecasters to predict the unforseen.
In a way which may be more tantalising than helpful, the unforseen events which impact on NZ interest rates and exchange rates tend to come from a small number of sources.

Monetary policy plays a large role, particularly in New Zealand. Other policies of government can also have a large influence but not in such a readily identifiable manner. And, clearly, trends in offshore markets have a huge influence.

At the moment, the expectation built into exchange rates and interest rates is for easier domestic monetary policy over the coming months, pushing short-term wholesale interest rates down below 8.0 percent by early 1997 and the NZ TWI modestly lower over the next 12 months.

It seems little weight is being given at present to the likelihood of higher offshore interest rates (given low inflation and only modest growth rates internationally) and/or a re-emergence of inflationary pressures.
It also seems, judging by the magnitude of the changes expected, that people are expecting some changes to the monetary policy framework.
Before discussing the risks associated with this outlook, it is worth stepping back and looking where NZ interest rates and exchange rates are.

First, wholesale NZ long-term interest rates at seven-point-something are now at levels more consistent with the size of the economy, our history of unstable government policies and our current high levels of offshore debt and current account deficit.
Coincidentally, these rates are similar to those in Australia. They provide a guide to where we can expect NZ short-term rates to eventually go.
Viewed from this perspective, it is NZ short-term rates, and hence still the majority of retail lending and deposit rates, which can be termed "high".
The reason for this appears to be the monetary policy framework -- we are having difficulties maintaining inflation below 2.0 percent.

It also appears reasonable to claim that our exchange rates -- although not all -- are "high" based on the levels now reached relative to our recent past and the trouble that these rates are causing exporters.
Whether these short-term rates and exchange rates do indeed decline over the next six to 12 months, however, is not assured. This is where the unforeseen comes to play.

In these times of policy negotiation it is possible that changes occur to the monetary policy framework and to other government policies which allow the Reserve Bank to ease conditions to the extent currently priced into interest rates
and exchange rates.

After all, these would only reduce our short-term rates to levels more consistent with those in similar countries offshore. However, without such changes, a number of forces are likely to emerge next year to prevent interest rate declines of the magnitude expected.
The Reserve Bank is currently forecasting underlying inflation to be around 1.0 percent by mid 1997. However, this is under very different monetary conditions than that priced into rates at present.
And, as the Governor recently warned, boosts to demand by looser fiscal policy will only accentuate the risk of higher inflation.
Under the current policy framework, a more modest interest rate decline is likely but possibly still a modest exchange rate decline.
Which brings to mind another axiom of forecasting: predict the trend over a time period, possibly predict a level eventually attained, but never try to specify both a level and a date.

Hence, the best that can be said at present is that short-term interest rates are declining, they may eventually reach 7.0 percent and NZ exchange rates are still rising at present but the trend will probably be flat-to-downwards next year.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
